steps.intent: Slovenia’s objective is a consensus-oriented text that reaffirms sustaining peace, national ownership, conflict prevention, inclusive participation, and stronger links among the Peacebuilding Commission, the Security Council, and financing partners. The main expected difficulties will be language on human rights, climate-related risks, and civil society participation, which Slovenia will need to balance against the sensitivities of permanent members while preserving a text capable of adoption without veto.

messages.Algeria: Algeria thanks Slovenia for the balanced draft and supports its overall orientation. We ask for clearer recognition of the African Union and other regional organizations, and for language preventing political conditionalities in peacebuilding support. We also seek an operative call for predictable financing and a reference to the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement in the climate paragraph.
messages.China: China supports the draft's emphasis on national ownership, host-State consent and respect for sovereignty. We ask that development and poverty eradication be explicitly recognized as foundations of sustaining peace, that human rights language not be applied selectively or against national circumstances, and that UN coordination respect the mandates of the principal organs. With these adjustments, China can support the text.
messages.Denmark: Denmark supports Slovenia's balanced draft as a good basis and can support it with targeted strengthening. We ask in particular that OP4 remove the 'national circumstances' qualifier and anchor women's and youth participation at all stages, and that PP8 recognise climate change and environmental degradation as risk multipliers for peace and security. We also seek a safe and enabling environment for civil society and a clearer operative call for predictable and sustainable peacebuilding financing.
messages.France: France welcomes the Slovenian draft and supports it as a good basis. We would like the text to recognise more clearly that climate and environmental factors can exacerbate risks to peace and security, and to ensure civil society participation and prevention of sexual and gender-based violence in OP4. We also suggest a minor strengthening of OP3 on inclusive and accountable institutions.
messages.Greece: Greece supports the draft as a balanced basis and thanks Slovenia for the text. We ask for two targeted additions: climate sensitivity in OP4 and financing in the OP5 reporting request. We can accept the remainder as drafted.
messages.Guyana: Guyana welcomes the balanced draft and supports consensus. As a climate-vulnerable small island developing State, we ask the penholder to strengthen the climate-security language in PP8 and to include climate-related security risks in OP5, with the existing safeguards on mandates. We also suggest adding 'flexible' to the financing language in PP6. With those adjustments, Guyana can join consensus.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the draft’s emphasis on national ownership, sovereignty and host-State consent. We ask that PP4 clearly preserve the respective mandates of the General Assembly and ECOSOC, that PP6 anchor climate references in the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement, and that OP5 include reporting on predictable peacebuilding financing. These changes would strengthen consensus and implementation.
messages.Panama: Panama supports the balanced text and its emphasis on national ownership, prevention, and inclusive participation. We would like the climate reference strengthened and the Secretary-General’s reporting to explicitly cover financing for peacebuilding, within existing mandates. We can support the text with those modifications.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea supports the draft as circulated. It reflects our priorities of national ownership, integrated UN action, conflict prevention, and the full and meaningful participation of women and youth. We are ready to join consensus on this text.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation supports the draft’s core reaffirmation of national ownership, sovereignty, and host-State consent. We cannot accept language that could imply assessed contributions for peacebuilding, and we need the climate-related paragraph to avoid securitization and remain within respective mandates. We also ask for more balanced, nationally grounded language on gender and human rights.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone supports the overall balance of the draft, including its emphasis on national ownership and coherence. We would like the 2025 review to have operative follow-up on predictable and sustainable peacebuilding financing, including the Peacebuilding Fund, and a clearer reference to the Peacebuilding Commission's role in transition and mission drawdown contexts. We are flexible on exact wording but consider these points important for implementation.
messages.Somalia: Somalia supports the overall balance of the Slovenian draft, especially its reaffirmation of national ownership and sovereignty. We ask the penholder to add an operative paragraph on adequate, predictable and sustainable peacebuilding financing, explicitly recognize the African Union and IGAD in partnership language, and reflect terrorism and violent extremism among the complex challenges in PP7. These amendments are important for countries emerging from conflict, including Somalia, and can be accommodated within existing mandates.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom welcomes the balanced Slovenian draft and can support it with targeted strengthening. We ask the penholder to align the participation language in PP6 with applicable international law and to add civil society to OP4, reflecting the Council's consistent support for safe and meaningful participation. We would also support referencing climate-related security risks in the operational paragraph on conflict sensitivity.
messages.United States of America: The United States supports the draft's emphasis on national ownership, host-State consent, and conflict prevention, but we cannot accept references to assessed contributions or climate change in this context. We also need language confirming that any reporting or follow-up is within existing mandates and resources, and we ask that 'gender-responsive' be replaced with language focused on the specific needs and participation of women and girls. We are ready to work with the penholder on these adjustments.

steps.summary: The revised draft keeps the core agenda of national ownership, coherence and prevention, while removing explicit assessed-contribution and climate-change references to protect P5 consensus. It adds compromise financing language, AU/IGAD recognition, development language and stronger participation/SGBV provisions. Broad support is expected, with one elected member possibly opposing and one abstaining.

messages.Algeria: Algeria supports the current text and will join consensus. We welcome the incorporation of African Union partnership, the right to development, conditionality language and predictable financing. While we would have preferred an explicit reference to the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement, we will not press it at this stage and call for full implementation of the resolution.
messages.China: China supports the current text, which is balanced and reaffirms national ownership, sovereignty and non-interference, while recognizing development as essential to sustaining peace. We appreciate the penholder’s incorporation of our proposals on human rights qualifiers, mandate-respecting UN coordination and financing without new assessed obligations, and we have no further changes to request.
messages.Denmark: Denmark thanks Slovenia for the revised text and welcomes the inclusion of participation, civil society, SGBV and financing. Our remaining red line is OP5: the qualifier “national legislation, priorities and circumstances” must not weaken the full, equal, meaningful and safe participation of women, youth and civil society; please replace it with “in accordance with relevant resolutions and applicable international law.” On PP8, we still need explicit recognition that climate change can act as a risk multiplier for peace and security, as previously requested.
messages.France: France thanks the penholder and welcomes the inclusion of civil society, sexual and gender-based violence, and inclusive and accountable institution-building. We continue to believe that a 2025 peacebuilding text cannot omit climate change as a risk multiplier. France therefore requests the reintroduction of climate-exacerbation language in the adverse-effects paragraph and is ready to support the text once this is reflected.
messages.Greece: Greece supports the revised draft as a balanced compromise and welcomes the inclusion of financing for peacebuilding in OP6. We continue to believe that climate-sensitive language would strengthen peacebuilding efforts, but in the interest of Council unity and in light of P5 concerns we will not insist on it at this stage. Greece is ready to join consensus.
messages.Guyana: Guyana thanks the penholder for accepting flexible financing and supports the draft with the following refinements. As a small island developing State, we cannot ignore the climate-security nexus; we ask that PP9 explicitly recognize climate change and SIDS vulnerabilities, and that OP6 include climate-related security risks in the Secretary-General's reporting. These are important for our delegation, and we will work constructively to preserve Council unity.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan appreciates the penholder’s acceptance of language on respective mandates and financing. We continue to believe that a reference to the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement is important in the environmental-degradation paragraph, given the climate vulnerability of many peacebuilding contexts. With this addition, Pakistan can support the text.
messages.Panama: Panama welcomes the acceptance of financing reporting in OP6. We still believe PP8 should explicitly recognize climate change and climate-risk assessments, given their cross-border and conflict-risk impacts; this remains an important but non-blocking request. If retained, Panama can support the text, and we would not block consensus solely on this point.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea supports the revised draft and commends the penholder for preserving a balanced text. We welcome its emphasis on national ownership, conflict prevention, inclusive participation of women and youth, and predictable financing within existing mandates. We have no further changes and encourage the Council to adopt the text by consensus.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation notes that the revised text reflects our key concerns on national ownership, sovereignty, non-interference, and the need to avoid new assessed obligations. The financing safeguards and nationally grounded language on gender and human rights are welcome. We are prepared to support the draft as it stands and encourage a consensus outcome.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone supports the revised text as a balanced basis for consensus. Our key priorities on predictable financing, timely Peacebuilding Fund access, and the Peacebuilding Commission's transition role have been reflected; while we would have preferred the financing options report to include assessed funding, we will not block consensus on that point.
messages.Somalia: Somalia thanks the penholder for incorporating our key concerns, including the explicit reference to the African Union and IGAD, the recognition of terrorism and transnational organized crime, and the call for adequate, predictable and sustainable financing for nationally led priorities. The revised text upholds national ownership, sovereignty and non-interference while strengthening partnership with regional organizations. Somalia therefore supports the current draft and encourages the Council to adopt it by consensus.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom supports the current text. We welcome the inclusion of language on applicable international law, including international human rights law, and on the participation of civil society, which reflect our key priorities. We encourage all members to join consensus so the Council can send a unified message on implementing the peacebuilding and sustaining peace agenda.
messages.United States of America: We appreciate the penholder’s efforts to reflect our concerns on assessed contributions and climate language. The United States can support the text with the following adjustments: remove the prohibition on political conditionality in OP4, delete the reference to the right to development, and soften OP3’s call to scale up financing to an encouragement. These changes are necessary to preserve donor flexibility and ensure the resolution does not create new financial or legal obligations.

reasons.Algeria: Algeria indicated support and secured retention of its priorities on national ownership, AU/IGAD partnership, and financing without new assessed obligations. The draft is consistent with Algeria’s positions, so it votes in favour.
reasons.China: China’s last negotiation position was support, with no changes requested, and the penholder confirmed that sovereignty, national ownership, and the no-new-assessed-obligations principle were preserved. Voting in favour maintains Council unity while the statement reinforces China’s key interpretive concerns.
reasons.Denmark: Denmark is a strong supporter of the UN peacebuilding and sustaining peace agenda, and its red-line request on OP5 was accepted. Although its climate language preference was only partially reflected, the overall resolution advances Danish priorities on prevention, inclusion, human rights and multilateral cooperation.
reasons.France: France sought explicit climate-change language in PP9, and the penholder accepted it; the revised text is consistent with France’s support for the peacebuilding and sustaining peace agenda. France therefore votes in favour and uses the opportunity to explain its position before the vote.
reasons.Greece: Greece was already in support and the text reflects its priorities on multilateralism, national ownership, coherence, climate sensitivity, and financing within existing mandates. A short explanation in favour is consistent with its constructive Council role.
reasons.Guyana: Guyana’s key priorities on SIDS and climate-related security reporting were substantially reflected, and as an elected member it would support a broadly consensus peacebuilding text despite the weaker preambular wording.
reasons.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the draft overall because it upholds national ownership, sovereignty, and voluntary rather than new assessed financing. Its requested UNFCCC/Paris reference was important but not a red line, so Pakistan votes in favour while clarifying its climate position.
reasons.Panama: Panama had requested stronger climate language and climate-risk assessments, which were accepted, and the balanced draft aligns with its support for national ownership, multilateral cooperation, and predictable peacebuilding financing without new assessed obligations.
reasons.Republic of Korea: Republic of Korea supported the balanced draft without requesting changes, so it votes in favour and sees no need for a pre-vote explanation.
reasons.Russian Federation: The draft preserves Russia’s key conditions on national sovereignty and no new assessed obligations, and Moscow already supported it in the final negotiation round. A pre-vote explanation is therefore unnecessary.
reasons.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone had already indicated support and has strong national and regional interests in peacebuilding financing, national ownership, and the Peacebuilding Commission. The amended text preserves the key elements it sought, so it should vote in favour with a short explanation before the vote.
reasons.Slovenia: Slovenia is the sponsor of this balanced draft and would vote in favour, consistent with its priorities on multilateralism, human rights, gender equality, climate security and national ownership. Speaking before the vote allows it to explain its support and encourage consensus.
reasons.Somalia: Somalia’s last position was support, it requested no changes, and its key priorities—national ownership, AU/IGAD partnership, counterterrorism, and financing—are retained. Voting in favour is consistent with its national interest in conflict-affected countries and its constructive Council role.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The text aligns with UK priorities and the United Kingdom supported the previous resolution on this agenda item. The accepted language on international law and civil society participation addresses its key concerns, so the United Kingdom should vote in favour.
reasons.United States of America: The draft incorporates the U.S. red-line and key requested changes, including national-priorities language and softened financing language, while preserving U.S. priorities and avoiding new assessed obligations. The United States would therefore support the resolution and explain its vote before the vote.

before.Algeria: Algeria votes in favour of this draft resolution. We welcome its reaffirmation of national ownership and the primary responsibility of national Governments in defining peacebuilding priorities, as well as its clear respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity, political independence and non-interference in internal affairs. We also value the recognition of the role of the African Union, IGAD and other regional and subregional organizations, and the emphasis on predictable and sustainable financing without creating new assessed obligations. Algeria encourages full implementation of resolution 2282 (2016) and General Assembly resolution 70/262 and remains committed to an integrated, coherent and nationally led approach to sustaining peace.
before.China: China votes in favour of the draft resolution. We welcome that the text reaffirms national ownership and the primary responsibility of national Governments, respects the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of States, and clearly states that no new assessed obligations will be created. We hope that implementation will continue to respect the mandates of the principal organs of the United Nations, including the budgetary authority of the General Assembly, and will focus on supporting nationally identified priorities and the needs of the countries concerned.
before.Denmark: Denmark will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We welcome a balanced text that reaffirms national ownership, conflict prevention, inclusive participation and the central role of the United Nations peacebuilding architecture. We are pleased that our red-line concern in OP5 has been met by anchoring efforts in applicable international law, including international human rights law. We would have preferred stronger language recognising climate change, environmental degradation and food insecurity as risk multipliers for peace and security, but the text nonetheless contains important climate-related language and constitutes a constructive step in implementing the sustaining peace agenda. Denmark therefore supports the resolution.
before.France: France welcomes the draft resolution and the constructive spirit in which it was negotiated. We welcome in particular the recognition that climate change can exacerbate existing risks to peace and security, as well as the emphasis on national ownership, the full and meaningful participation of women and youth, and predictable and sustainable financing for peacebuilding within existing mandates and without creating new assessed obligations. France will vote in favour.
before.Greece: Greece welcomes the draft resolution and will vote in favour. We strongly support the peacebuilding and sustaining peace agenda, including an integrated and coherent United Nations approach, national ownership, conflict prevention, and adequate, predictable and sustainable financing without creating new assessed obligations. We also value the references to gender-sensitive and climate-sensitive approaches, which are essential to addressing contemporary risks to peace and security.
before.Guyana: Guyana will vote in favour of the draft resolution. We welcome the inclusion of language on the particular vulnerabilities of small island developing States and on climate-related security risks in reporting. While we would have preferred stronger preambular language on the adverse effects of climate change, we see this text as a balanced and constructive basis for advancing nationally owned peacebuilding and sustaining peace. We stress that adequate, predictable, flexible and sustainable financing remains essential, including for prevention and for the special circumstances of small island developing States.
before.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the draft resolution and will vote in favour. We thank the penholder for the inclusive consultations and for retaining the centrality of national ownership, sovereignty and non-interference, as well as the primary responsibility of national authorities in peacebuilding. We would have preferred an explicit reference to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement in the climate-related provisions, since climate change is a serious risk multiplier, particularly for developing countries. Nonetheless, Pakistan joins consensus in support of the full and effective implementation of resolution 2282 (2016) and the sustaining peace agenda.
before.Panama: Panama will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We welcome the incorporation of our concerns on recognizing the adverse effects of climate change and environmental degradation, including through climate-risk assessments, which are especially important for small island developing States and other vulnerable countries. Panama supports a coherent, nationally owned and nationally led approach to peacebuilding and sustaining peace, with predictable and sustainable financing that respects the mandates of United Nations organs and the budgetary authority of the General Assembly, and without creating new assessed obligations. We also value the emphasis on the full, equal and meaningful participation of women, youth and civil society, and we encourage continued close cooperation among the Security Council, the General Assembly, ECOSOC, the Peacebuilding Commission and the Peacebuilding Fund.
before.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone thanks the delegation of Slovenia for its efforts to bring the Council together on this important agenda. As a country with direct experience of peacebuilding and sustaining peace, Sierra Leone supports a nationally owned and nationally led approach, with adequate and predictable financing for peacebuilding, including continued and flexible access to the Peacebuilding Fund. We also value the role of the Peacebuilding Commission, the participation of women and youth, and stronger partnerships with regional and subregional organizations, including the African Union. We believe this draft resolution offers a balanced basis for further implementation of the peacebuilding and sustaining peace agenda, and Sierra Leone will vote in favour.
before.Slovenia: Slovenia will vote in favour of this draft resolution, which we were honoured to table. It reflects a carefully balanced approach grounded in national ownership, an integrated whole-of-system response, and the centrality of conflict prevention, inclusive dialogue and the full, equal and meaningful participation of women, youth and civil society. We particularly welcome its attention to predictable and sustainable financing without creating new assessed obligations, and to conflict-sensitive, risk-informed approaches, including climate-related security risks. We thank all partners for their constructive engagement and call for united support for its implementation.
before.Somalia: Somalia votes in favour of this draft resolution. As a country emerging from conflict and as an elected member of this Council, we reaffirm the centrality of national ownership, sovereignty, and national priorities in peacebuilding and sustaining peace. We welcome the retention of references to the African Union, IGAD, terrorism, and predictable and sustainable financing, and we underscore the need for timely and flexible support through the Peacebuilding Fund for nationally identified priorities. We also stress the full, equal, and meaningful participation of women, youth, and civil society, and the importance of coherent United Nations action within existing mandates and without creating new assessed obligations.
before.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom votes in favour of this draft resolution. We welcome its balanced reaffirmation of national ownership and the primary responsibility of the Security Council, alongside the importance of an integrated approach across the United Nations system. We strongly support the emphasis on conflict prevention, the full, equal and meaningful participation of women, youth and civil society, human rights and the rule of law, and predictable voluntary financing for peacebuilding without creating new assessed obligations. We encourage full implementation within existing mandates and in full respect of the respective roles of United Nations organs.
before.United States of America: Thank you, Mr. President. The United States supports this resolution. We appreciate the penholder’s engagement and the revisions made to affirm that peacebuilding priorities must be nationally owned and nationally led, and that financing should be enhanced as appropriate through voluntary contributions without creating new assessed obligations or new mandates. We also welcome the resolution’s practical focus on conflict prevention, coherence, and the advisory role of the Peacebuilding Commission. At the same time, we stress that references to climate-related security risks and other complex challenges must be implemented within existing mandates and resources, with full respect for national sovereignty and the budgetary authority of the General Assembly. The United States will vote in favour.

after.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea voted in favour of this resolution and welcomes its adoption by consensus. We believe it provides a balanced and practical basis for advancing the peacebuilding and sustaining peace agenda. The Republic of Korea reaffirms the importance of the full, effective and accelerated implementation of resolution 2282 (2016) and General Assembly resolution 70/262, with national ownership at the centre. Peacebuilding must be nationally led and nationally owned, while the United Nations system, including the Peacebuilding Commission and the Peacebuilding Fund, should support nationally identified priorities in a coherent, flexible and accountable manner within existing mandates. We also stress the importance of conflict prevention, inclusive dialogue, the full, equal and meaningful participation of women and youth, respect for human rights and the rule of law, and conflict-sensitive, risk-informed approaches, including with regard to climate-related risks. We encourage continued efforts to mobilize adequate, predictable and sustainable financing, including through voluntary contributions and partnerships, without creating new assessed obligations. The Republic of Korea will continue to support the implementation of this resolution and to work with all Council members and partners to sustain peace.
after.Russian Federation:
Mr. President,

The Russian Federation voted in favour of the draft resolution submitted by Slovenia. We welcome the fact that the text, in its final version, is balanced and reaffirms the central principles that must guide peacebuilding and sustaining peace: national ownership, the primary responsibility of national Governments, respect for the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of States, and non-interference in their internal affairs.

We note that the resolution clearly states that no new assessed obligations are created. Financing for peacebuilding must remain voluntary and predictable, within existing mandates and resources, and in full respect for the budgetary authority of the General Assembly. We also emphasize that the provisions of this resolution must not be interpreted as creating new mandates for the Security Council, the Secretariat or any other United Nations body.

Peacebuilding cannot be effective if it is transformed into a tool of external pressure, political conditionality or interference in domestic affairs. References to human rights, civil society, climate-related risks and participation must be implemented strictly in accordance with applicable international obligations, national legislation and the respective mandates of United Nations organs. The Security Council must not duplicate the work of other bodies or securitize development, humanitarian and climate issues.

The Russian Federation remains committed to the implementation of resolution 2282 (2016), General Assembly resolution 70/262 and resolution 2413 (2018). We are ready to continue constructive work on the basis of respect for the Charter and the sovereign choices of States.
after.Slovenia: Thank you, Mr. President. Slovenia warmly welcomes the unanimous adoption of this resolution and thanks all Council members for their constructive engagement and support. As penholder, we believe this text reflects a carefully balanced consensus: it reaffirms national ownership and the primary responsibility of national authorities, while underscoring the need for an integrated and coherent United Nations response centred on conflict prevention, inclusive dialogue and the full, equal and meaningful participation of women, youth and civil society. We also welcome the emphasis on predictable and sustainable financing for nationally led peacebuilding priorities, including through voluntary contributions and timely access to the Peacebuilding Fund, without creating new assessed obligations. Slovenia remains committed to working with all partners to ensure the full and effective implementation of resolution 2282 (2016), General Assembly resolution 70/262 and this resolution, including through conflict-sensitive and risk-informed approaches. The unanimous support shown today is a strong signal of the Council’s shared commitment to sustaining peace. Thank you.
